short_definition: Kaizen is a Japanese philosophy of continuous improvement that focuses on making small, regular, incremental changes to habits, processes or work rather than relying on big one-off overhauls.
explanation: Kaizen means making one small improvement at a time and repeating the process. The word roughly translates as 'improvement' or 'change for the better', and it became widely known through Japanese manufacturing and lean production. In personal life, it means choosing one small, specific change, trying it, reviewing the result and repeating, often as a plan-do-check-act cycle.

Kaizen matters because small changes are easier to start and keep up than dramatic resolutions, and the gains build over time, much like compound interest. It also makes change less intimidating: a five-minute daily habit feels far easier than overhauling your whole life.

The trade-off is that small tweaks can't fix everything. Some problems need a bigger decision, such as changing jobs, ending a contract or rebuilding a broken process, and endlessly polishing small details can become a way to avoid it. Kaizen also needs honest measurement, because without tracking you can't tell whether a change is helping.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): Instead of vowing to 'fix my finances', you spend 10 minutes each Sunday reviewing your spending and make one small change a week. Week one: cancel an unused $12 subscription. Week two: switch from a $40 phone plan to a $25 one. Week three: set up an automatic $50 monthly transfer to savings. After a month, you're spending $27 a month less on recurring bills and have an automatic $50-a-month savings habit.
common_mistake: Making several 'small' changes at once without tracking them, so you can't tell which ones worked. Improve one thing, measure it, then move to the next.
title: Kaizen (Continuous Improvement)
